newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ex-minister says no tougher austerity.
newsitem.headline: French ex-minister says no tougher austerity.

text.p: Ex-budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, a member of France's ruling centre-right coalition, ruled out on Wednesday any further austerity measures should it win snap elections, pledging tax cuts and economic growth.

Asked about opinion poll findings that most French voters expect tougher austerity should the bloc win May-June elections, Sarkozy of the Gaullist RPR, senior party in the ruling coalition, told RTL radio: "I regret this scepticism.

"There will not be tougher austerity, and no increase in taxes...Of all developed countries, we are the ones with the heaviest burden of taxes and we cannot go on like that," said Sarkozy, an ally of former prime minister Edouard Balladur who has long been lobbying for faster tax cuts.
Sarkozy said that reduced state deficits, lower taxes and respect of the criteria for a planned European single currency would all help boost economic growth.

"The Socialists say there is nothing more urgent than telling the French to work less. They say there aren't enough taxes on companies," Sarkozy said, a reference to the Socialist Party's advocacy of a cut in working hours.

He predicted the short campaign, launched by President Jacques Chirac on Monday, would highlight the divide between left-wing parties and the centre-right, adding that the far-right and anti-immigrant National Front had benefited in the past from the lack of such a confrontation.

As a symbol of reconciliation Balladur, who fought fellow-Gaullist Chirac in a fratricidal 1995 presidential election battle, was taken out of political isolation to attend a policy speech by Prime Minister Alain Juppe alongside other coalition leaders on Tuesday.

A CSA poll for the daily Le Parisien -- the first since Chirac called the election for May 25-June 1 -- foresaw the ruling coalition winning 332 seats in the National Assembly to 222 for the combined left-wing opposition.
It held a huge 464-seat majority in the outgoing assembly.
